stages.name: Positive and normative economics
stages.title: Positive and normative economics
stages.sub: Tell facts about the economy apart from opinions about what should be done, and see why opinions still shape policy.

steps.q: "Unemployment in the UK was 4.2% last year." Could two researchers with the same data end up disagreeing about whether this is true?
steps.right: No, the data would settle it either way
steps.hint: Is there a number out there that either matches this claim or does not?

steps.q: Take the claim about unemployment. Whoever is asked, does the data make it true or false, whatever anyone feels about it?
steps.wrong: No, it is true if enough agree
steps.hint: A number either matches the claim or it does not.

steps.q: "The government should cut unemployment benefits." Could two people who agree on every statistic still disagree about this?
steps.right: Yes, because it depends on what they value
steps.wrong: No, the statistics would settle it
steps.hint: Even with identical facts in front of them, could their views on fairness still differ?

steps.q: Take the claim about cutting benefits. It says what ought to happen. Could facts alone show it is right or wrong?
steps.right: No, it rests on views about what is fair
steps.wrong: Yes, the facts prove it right or wrong
steps.hint: Two people with the same facts can still disagree about what ought to be done.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms into the two chains that lead to one concept. Chain 1 is what evidence can settle. Chain 2 is what people believe should happen.
steps.then: what does telling the two apart give you?

steps.q: Compare "Raising the minimum wage will reduce jobs" with "Raising the minimum wage is right". Which could evidence settle?
steps.wrong: The second one, about what is right
steps.hint: One claims something measurable will happen. The other claims something ought to happen. Which is measurable?

steps.q: Two governments see the same evidence about a policy, yet one bans it and the other allows it. What explains the difference?
steps.right: Their differing opinions about what matters most
steps.wrong: They must be looking at different data
steps.hint: If the facts are identical, what else could differ between the two decisions?
